newsitem.title: ITALY: Prodi praises Berlusconi move on Italy mini-budget.
newsitem.headline: Prodi praises Berlusconi move on Italy mini-budget.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi praised opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi on Sunday for expressing willingness to back a mini-budget providing the measures helped Italy join the European single currency.

"The willingness shown by the leader of the Freedom Alliance, Silvio Berlusconi, to vote for the government's public finance provisions is an act of responsibility that does him honour," Prodi said in a statement.

"I am certain that, if confirmed, such a willingness will allow the country to achieve without pointless and dangerous conflicts the objectives needed to enter the single currency with the strongest European economies."

Newpapers had quoted Berlusconi as indicating his opposition might be prepared to help Prodi with a mini-budget needed to bring Italy's deficit down to levels that would enable the country to meet single currency requirements.
Berlusconi said the government would have to spell out clearly what it was trying to achieve and also address structural problems of public spending.
However the papers also quoted far-right National Alliance leader Gianfranco Fini, Berlusconi's main coalition partner, as declaring the government "untrustworthy".

"This is not a mini-budget but a colossal budget, a maxi-budget given that we are talking about 15 trillion lire," the La Stampa newspaper quoted former prime minister and billionaire media mogul Berlusconi as saying.
"However, if its contents are those that Europe demands of us, that is to say a structural reform of spending, we are available," said Berlusconi.

The government relies on the support of the hard-left Communist Refoundation party for a majority in parliament but that party has said it is opposed to the mini-budget and any cuts in public spending or tax hikes.
It has also called for a negotiated delay to the start of EMU and threatened to withdraw its support if the government cuts a deal with the opposition.
Massimo d'Alema, leader of the Democratic Party of the Left which is Prodi's main backer in parliament, warned Refoundation last month that it could not hold the government hostage.
Prodi said on Friday that his government would have an exact figure for the mini-budget within the next few weeks.
"I have said that, for now, we are looking at a figure that ranges between six trillion and 14.5 trillion lire," he said.
The Bank of Italy had said on Friday that 15 trillion lire must be sliced from the budget deficit if Italy was to cut its deficit to GDP ratio to the three percent required.
Prodi put the ratio at 3.3 to 3.4 percent at present and said the mini-budget would bring it down to three percent.
His government passed a tough 62.5 trillion lire 1997 budget at the end of last year as part of a campaign to ensure Italy is a founding member of EMU.

A decision on which countries will qualify for EMU founder membership will be made in early 1998 on the basis of their 1997 accounts. Countries must meet set targets on inflation, exchange rates, interest rates, deficits and public debt.
